Cada tema termina con sus ideas clave y: Each topic ends with its key ideas and its formulas. This page gathers them all, in the order of the map, so as to have them together when it is time to revise. It adds nothing: it collects.
Aquí están, juntas y en orden, todas las: Here, together and in order, are all the formulas and key ideas of the topics of your subject. They are not copied by hand: they come out of the topics themselves every time you open this page, so if a topic changes, the formula sheet changes with it.
Un formulario no es para aprender: es pa: A formula sheet is not for learning: it is for checking. If on reading a formula you do not remember where it comes from or when it is used, the name of the topic is a link; go back to it and do a couple of exercises. And it is worth making your own by hand: writing a formula forces you to decide what is important about it, and that is already studying.
Con el botón de imprimir sale una versió: The print button gives a clean version, with no menus or interactive examples, that can be saved as a PDF. Choose the subject first: Matemáticas II and MACS II do not have the same syllabus.
Ves en el formulario $|kA| = k^n|A|$ y n: You see $|kA| = k^n|A|$ on the formula sheet and cannot remember why. What do you do?
Una fórmula sin su porqué se recuerda ma: A formula without its reason is remembered badly and applied worse: in the exam it will turn up with $n = 3$ and $k = -2$ and you will have to know what to do with each part.
Seguir el enlace al tema y hacer un par: Follow the link to the topic and do a couple of exercises
Para eso está el enlace. Al multiplicar: That is what the link is for. Multiplying a matrix by $k$ multiplies all its rows, and each row contributes a factor: with that the formula rebuilds itself.
Saltarla, porque seguramente no cae: Skip it, because it probably will not come up
Cae. Es uno de los errores más frecuente: It does. It is one of the commonest mistakes in the exam, and it is in this block's catalogue of mistakes.
Los formularios tienen mala fama en clas: Formula sheets have a bad name in class, but mathematicians have always used them. Gradshteyn and Ryzhik's tables of integrals, published in Russian in 1943 and reissued to this day, run to more than a thousand pages, and Abramowitz and Stegun's Handbook of Mathematical Functions (1964) was for decades one of the most cited books in science. Its successor is today a public NIST website, the Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. Nobody knows all the formulas: what you know is which one to look up and how to check that it is the right one.
